## merge vs rebase

**merge** — join two branches, keep full history. Creates merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
     \
      D---E  feature
           \
            M  ← merge commit (has 2 parents)
```

**rebase** — replay feature commits on top of target. Linear history, no merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
             \
              D'--E'  ← replayed commits (new hashes)
```

---

## when use what

**use merge when:**
- public/shared branch (main, develop)
- want preserve exact history + context
- PR merges — shows when branch integrated
- team work, others pulled your branch

**use rebase when:**
- local cleanup before PR
- want linear, readable history
- pulling latest main into feature branch
- squashing WIP commits

---

## tradeoffs

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| history | exact, branchy | clean, linear |
| conflicts | once at merge | once per replayed commit |
| safety | safe on shared branches | **dangerous on shared branches** |
| blame/bisect | harder to trace | easier |
| commit hashes | preserved | **rewritten** |

---

## golden rule

> Never rebase commits already pushed to shared branch.

Rebase rewrites hashes → teammates' history diverge → pain.

---

## common patterns

```bash
# update feature branch with latest main (local only)
git checkout feature
git rebase main

# clean merge into main (preserves branch context)
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff feature

# interactive: squash WIP before PR
git rebase -i main
```

`--no-ff` force merge commit even when fast-forward possible. Good for explicit record of feature integration.
